title: Screens and attention
hookLine: a buzz on the table, and an old city with six gates and one gatekeeper
tomorrow: an old verse about a monkey knew the scroll. what did it see?

cards: A phone lies face up on the table. It buzzes once, and half a sentence from a group chat slides across the glass. Nobody touched it, and already the eyes have left the page.
Five minutes later, the page is still waiting, open at the same line. Now an older scene, from a sutta. A frontier city with strong walls and six gates.
A pair of swift messengers rides in from the east with an urgent message for the lord of the city. At the gate, someone steps out to meet them. Everything turns on who that is.

teach.b: The sutta names the figure: a gatekeeper, wise and capable, who keeps out strangers and lets in the ones he knows. Then the Buddha explains the picture. The city is this body.
The six gates are the six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the mind, which the suttas count as a sense too. The gatekeeper is mindfulness, sati in Pali.
Elsewhere the suttas give the practice a plain name: guarding the doors of the senses. On seeing a sight, you don't grab at it and chase its details. Here's the part worth telling a friend tonight.
In this picture the gates stay open. A city with its gates bricked shut starves; the messengers in the story come in through them.

The trouble the sutta warns about is a gate with nobody standing there. A screen is a gate that hardly ever closes, and every buzz is a knock. The old teaching doesn't ask anyone to throw a phone in a river.
It asks a smaller, harder question, many times a day: who's at the gate right now, a habit or you?

Guarding the door means a person is posted there. A message comes; mindfulness looks at it, then lets it in or sends it on its way. And the messengers who belong in the city, the sutta says, are calm and clear seeing.

how: Restraint of the senses is part of the gradual training described in the suttas; lay Buddhists often practice it on observance days and retreats by keeping fewer distractions and returning attention to the breath.

o: keeping your eyes lowered whenever someone is near
giving up phones and music completely, like a monk
choosing what comes in through eye and ear, moment by moment

games.q: the city in the sutta — tap the pairs.

s: guarding the senses means shutting them off
in the simile the gates stay open; a gatekeeper chooses what comes in.
the suttas count the mind as one of the six senses
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: six gates.
in the sutta, the gatekeeper keeps everyone out
he keeps out strangers and lets in the ones he knows.

games.q: your phone lights up mid-conversation with your grandmother. it might matter. the gatekeeper picture suggests what?
o: never look while someone's talking; screens are the enemy.
notice the knock, then choose: glance now, or after she's done.
check it at once; an open gate means let everything through.
games.why: in the sutta the gates stay open and a wise gatekeeper decides. the point is someone at the gate, not a gate bricked shut.

practice: Turn your phone face down, out of reach, and rest your eyes on one object near you: a cup, a plant, a corner of the window. Each time the eye wants to leave, notice the knock, and return to the cup.
Let mindfulness stand at that one gate for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Screens and attention: six gates, always open, and one gatekeeper, mindfulness, choosing what comes in.

orig.note: Pali: indriya-samvara, restraint or guarding of the sense faculties.

carryVoice: For the road: guard the door, and leave it open. Four days into the mind at home.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 35.245 (Kimsuka Sutta: the frontier city with six gates, the wise gatekeeper, the swift pair of messengers)
Digha Nikaya 2 and Majjhima Nikaya 27 (guarding the doors of the senses: on seeing a form, not grasping at its signs and features)
